headline: Find objects through sight, sound, and touch.
intro: I proposed an accessibility-focused object-finding concept and developed it with my team into a Unity mobile AR prototype.
context: University of Michigan · XR course project · November–December 2022
role: Concept originator and Unity/C# team developer; iterated through weekly peer playtests.

hero.alt: An illustrated phone guides toward a selected apple through an arrow, spatial sound, and an alignment vibration.
hero.caption: Three cues point toward one target. This illustration explains the original mobile interaction; it is not an application screenshot.

question.title: Can a phone help someone locate a nearby object?
question.text: Inspired by assistive technology, I proposed combining recognition with directional cues for people with vision impairments. The prototype explored that interaction through two complementary ways to define a target.

steps.title: Choose what to find
steps.text: Detect a common object with on-device YOLOv3-tiny, or label an uploaded image for reference tracking.

steps.title: Follow the direction
steps.text: Select or cycle targets. An arrow, spatial ping, and alignment vibration provide complementary feedback.

steps.title: Keep controls accessible
steps.text: Use spoken labels and accessible controls, then stop guidance when the search is finished.

gallery.alt: Diagram of object detection and image references converging into one target-selection and guidance workflow.
gallery.caption: The two modes address different targets: recognizable object categories and specific visual references.

finding.title: Make the core search interaction work together.
finding.text: Peer playtests confirmed working audio and vibration but exposed confusion between modes. The team prioritized integrating those flows and polishing the interface; a radar-map prototype was deferred.

details: The browser demo reconstructs the interaction with a synthetic scene. The linked team trailer records the original mobile application.
Peer playtests informed the design. They do not establish validated effectiveness for people with vision impairments.
credits: A University of Michigan student-team project, developed in Unity with AR Foundation, Barracuda, and Apple accessibility support.
